home.content:
CRUMB & CO · THIS WEEK'S COVER · ISSUE NO. 118

Bread That Keeps Baker's Hours

The bake starts at 11pm and the queue starts at 7. Everything between those two numbers is what this week's issue is about.

A neighbourhood sourdough bakery on Marrow Lane, where the ovens work the night shift and the neighbourhood answers with its coats on. This week we follow one loaf from a jar of starter named Doris to the paper bag it leaves in.

Loaf of the Week: The Marrow Lane Country Loaf

Twenty per cent wholemeal, twenty per cent rye, the rest stoneground white from a mill two counties over. It is proved for eighteen hours in the cold, scored down the middle at four in the morning and baked on stone at 250°C for forty minutes, which is why the crust cracks like a floorboard when it cools.

The flavour is not shy. There is a sourness at the front, a nuttiness underneath from the rye, and a finish that tastes faintly of the flour's own field. Cut it thick, toast it until the edges catch, and put salted butter on it while it is still warm enough to melt.

We bake two hundred of these a day. They sell out by half past ten on a Saturday and by noon on a Tuesday. If you want one held back, Reserve a loaf and we will put your name on a bag.

The Overnight Bake, in Six Frames

23:00 — Doris comes out of the fridge. The starter is ten years old this spring and smells of yoghurt and green apples.

23:40 — Flour meets water. Nothing else for the first hour; the dough does the work of hydrating itself.

01:15 — The folds. Four sets, thirty minutes apart, each one turning the dough over on the bench like a bedsheet.

03:00 — Shaping. Two bakers, one bench, and a rhythm that only sounds like silence from the street.

04:20 — The score. A single cut down the middle with a blade held at a shallow angle, and the loaf decides how it opens.

06:15 — The first tray out. Thirty minutes to cool, forty minutes until the door opens.

“People think they come for the bread. They come because someone handed it to them warm and said their name.”
— Alina Marsh, who has worked the morning counter since the shop was a market stall

Field Notes from the Counter

07:02 — The first customer is a man with a bicycle who buys a country loaf and a flat white and reads the same page of his book until he finishes his coffee.

07:48 — A woman asks whether the seeded rye is suitable for a lunchbox. It is. She takes two.

08:30 — The school run arrives in a burst. Four croissants, one cinnamon bun, one very small child who is allowed to choose.

09:15 — The Friday-only pastries are gone by now, always. Ask us on a Thursday and we will say the same thing.

10:40 — The last country loaf goes to a man in paint-streaked trousers who says it is for his brother. We do not ask further.

Get the Next Issue While It's Warm

Reserve a loaf for collection any morning this week, or come to the door on Marrow Lane and take whatever is on the shelf. The menu changes with the day; the starter does not.
